# Current law — shipping-ci

**GENERATED by `pnpm governance:compile`. Never hand-edit (RULING 92).**
Governance snapshot `02758e3766628c73`. 28 rule(s) in force.

This file carries CURRENT law for this domain and nothing else. Superseded
wording is not here — it is in `docs/governance/history.md`, which explains
and never governs (RULING 172).

Authority precedence is RULING 185. The root constitution is `CLAUDE.md`.

## RULING 1 — merge cadence

*`R-0001` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-19 · also cited as `RULING 1`, `R1`, `R-1`*

- **sets** `shipping.promotion_path` = `integrated-head-merges-to-main`

ONE planned code merge per session. A second is permitted only to fix a
regression the live walk caught, and when one is taken the report names the
regression and states both SHAs. Close-out records — `state.md`, the tracker,
anything carrying the deploy SHA or the walk numbers — may follow as separate
named commits, because a document cannot name the commit that contains it.

**Status: LAW.** Written into `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-08-19 and amended
2026-08-20.

## RULING 56 — a scheduled job that fails tells someone

*`R-0056` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-21 · also cited as `RULING 56`, `R56`, `R-56`*


*Adopted 2026-08-21 (NH Hunt 3). Authoritative account: `docs/state.md`. Shipped
as `lib/ops/job-watch.ts`, `scripts/watch-workflows.mts` and
`.github/workflows/job-watch.yml`.*

**A degrading data path may not be a page nobody watches.**

The measurement that produced it: `refresh-meetings-snapshot` had failed **14 of
36** runs, `intake-tripwire` 2 of 8, `refresh-dotgov-snapshot` 1 of 8 — a third
nobody had named. The watcher runs daily at 15:40 UTC, after the other jobs have
had their slot. **Two consecutive failures opens a Needs Sean row. It never
resolves one.**

Proved without breaking anything to prove it: `--asof` holds the detector against
a window whose outcome is already known.

*Later measurement, NJ Hunt 4 (2026-08-22):* the detector's sampling was too
narrow to see a 17-in-40 failure rate and was widened — see RULING 82, which
closes `JOB01`.

## RULING 75 — a close-out commit is gated like any other commit to `main`

*`R-0075` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-22 · also cited as `RULING 75`, `R75`, `R-75`*

(Adopted 2026-08-22, the author's ruling, NJ Hunt 3. Written into law here
2026-08-22, NJ Hunt 4 item 1.3, closing `NS03`. It sits beside RULING 62 because
both are about a protection that reported green while not running.)

**Every commit that reaches `main` passes the same gate, and a close-out record
is a commit that reaches `main`.**

The merge-cadence rule above permits a session to ship its code once and then
write close-out records as separate named commits, because a document cannot
name the commit that contains it. That is correct and it stays. What went
unnoticed is what it implies about gating: `pnpm handoff --ship` calls itself the
single door everything merges through, and **for code it is — for close-out
records it never was.** They were committed after the ship and pushed straight
to `main` through no gate at all, by every session in this repo's history.

The shape put a red suite on `main` twice. The second time, NJ Hunt 2's close-out
carried a session script with five `TS18046` sites, build checks #196 and #197
failed, Netlify refused both deploys at 'building site', and production served a
seven-hour-old build for the rest of the day. **The session reported green gates
truthfully** — it ran them before the file existed. That is the failure this rule
exists to name: an honest report about a tree that no longer matched what was on
the server.

Three parts, and the third is the one nothing local could ever have supplied:

1. **`pnpm closeout` is the gated door.** It refuses off `main`, refuses a dirty
   tree, runs the literal build command `netlify.toml` gives Netlify — which
   type-checks everything `tsconfig.json` includes, `scripts/` included — pushes
   through `scripts/push-main.mjs`, then waits for the tip to go green. **There
   is no skip flag**, for the reason the build gate already gives: an escape
   hatch on a gate is how the gate stops meaning anything.
2. **`pnpm main:green` asks GitHub, not the working tree.** Every other gate in
   this repo answers a question about local files. The question that went unasked
   is about the REMOTE BRANCH, and only the server knows what happened to a
   commit after it landed. Four verdicts are kept apart — green, red, pending and
   **could-not-tell** — because a check that cannot reach its subject must never
   print like a passing one (RULING 24).
3. **`pnpm handoff` carries a `main checks` line and fails on RED.** A session
   may not report clean gates while leaving `main` failing and production stale.

*Why not a pre-push hook.* `core.hooksPath` is per-clone and can be silently
absent in a fresh clone, and a hook that runs on every work-in-progress push is a
hook that gets `--no-verify`d out of existence. The server-truth check has
neither problem — it cannot be absent, and it costs one API call.

*Why not a pre-push hook.* `buildGate()`'s header already rejected one and the

## RULING 77 — verify locally, ship once

*`R-0077` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-22 · also cited as `RULING 77`, `R77`, `R-77`*

(Adopted 2026-08-22, the author's ruling, NJ Hunt 4. It is the merge-cadence
rule's missing half: that rule says how many times a session may ship, and this
says WHEN.)

**Never ship and then verify. Verify, confirm it works, then ship.**

Almost nothing needs production. Screenshots at 430×932, `pnpm walk:all`, the
card checks, the who-governs pill and the whole ballot page all run against a
**local production build**. Only the deploy-SHA confirmation and `/api/build`
require the live site, because only those two are questions about what the server
is serving.

- **One planned deploy, one merge**, and close-out records are part of that
  commit where they can be.
- **A defect found in local verification is fixed BEFORE the ship**, not shipped
  and then patched. The second-merge exception in the merge-cadence rule above
  survives — a live walk that catches a regression must be allowed to fix it —
  but a session that could have caught the defect locally and did not has spent
  the exception on its own carelessness, and the report says so.

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance.* Ship-
then-verify was costing a merge every time, and the merges were not the real
price: between the ship and the verification, production was serving the defect
to readers. A local production build is the same bytes. There was never a reason
to find out on the live site.

The merge-cadence rule's second-merge exception survives — a live walk that
catches a regression must be allowed to fix it — but a session that could have
caught the defect locally and did not has spent the exception on its own
carelessness, and the report says so.

*What it supersedes:* nothing. It is the merge-cadence rule's missing half. That
rule said how many times a session may ship; this says when.

*The cost it removes:* between the ship and the verification, production was
serving the defect to readers. NJ Hunt 3 spent four of its seven code merges
exactly there. A local production build is the same bytes.

## RULING 78 — CI runs where it earns its cost

*`R-0078` · AMENDED · author_confirmed · 2026-08-22 · also cited as `RULING 78`, `R78`, `R-78`*

(Adopted 2026-08-22, the author's ruling, NJ Hunt 4.)

**A gate that runs three times for one merge is one gate and two copies of it.**

Build check was firing on the branch push, again on the pull request, and again
on the merge to `main` — three runs plus a Netlify deploy each, on top of the
scheduled refreshes. That exhausted the Actions balance, and an exhausted balance
does not fail loudly: it produced completed jobs with zero steps recorded, which
read as a broken tree for a whole session (`NS04`).

- **Build check runs on the pull request and on `main`.** The branch-push trigger
  is removed. Those two together cover everything the third covered, because
  every branch that matters becomes a pull request and every merge lands on
  `main`.
- **Scheduled refresh workflows run ONCE DAILY**, except the clerk filing near a
  filing deadline, which keeps its one-day RULING 53 clock.
- **Nothing stops gating.** This removes duplicate runs of the same check, never
  a check. A cadence change that dropped coverage would be the budget raised to
  fit the change it was supposed to catch, in another costume.

## RULING 113 — a step that reports success is asked whether it did the thing

*`R-0113` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-23 · also cited as `RULING 113`, `R113`, `R-113`*

(Adopted 2026-08-23, item 9. It is the **operation-count rule** — *an operation
that can return nothing must be asked what it returned* — pointed at a BUILD
STEP rather than at a data fetch. Supersedes nothing.)

**Where a step's product can be observed, observe it AT THE STEP, not at the
first consumer.**

`main` was red at `3d453fd` with four failures and one cause:
`NO CHROMIUM INSTALLED. Wanted build 1234; searched /home/runner/.cache/ms-playwright`.
The step before them, whose entire job is installing that browser, **reported
success in 27 seconds** — and its own log, two screens above the failure, reads
`Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.34 ... downloaded to /home/runner/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1234`.

**The install landed in exactly the directory the suite searched.** What failed
was `lib/ops/chromium-pin.ts`, looking for the binary at the legacy
`chrome-linux/chrome` while Chrome for Testing puts it at
`chrome-linux64/chrome`. It had never worked on any platform with the pinned
Playwright, the author's own Windows machine included.

Two separable failures, and the second is the one that cost the time:

1. **A step reported success with its product unchecked**, so the defect
   surfaced eighty seconds later inside four unrelated tests, after a
   2,000-test suite had already run.
2. **The message named the wrong half.** *"NO CHROMIUM INSTALLED"* about a
   directory holding a freshly installed Chromium sends every reader to the
   installer, which was working perfectly. An absence that can name what it DID
   see points at the reader instead of the writer.

So: a step whose product is observable carries a check immediately after it,
naming what it looked for, where, and what it found. **Where the product can be
compared against what the TOOL ITSELF reports producing, compare them** — that
is the drift check nothing had here, and the only one that could have failed.
`scripts/assert-browser.mts` is the instance; the rule is the class.

**The check has no skip flag**, for the reason the build gate already gives: an
escape hatch on a gate is how the gate stops meaning anything. The one locally
available "fix" — letting the guard pass with no browser — is what
`scripts/browser.mts` forbids in as many words.

<details>
<summary>The other hand-written copy of this rule, from <code>docs/rulings.md</code> — preserved verbatim</summary>

*Two copies of this rule were maintained by hand and they diverged. Neither was complete.
The fuller one is above; this is the other, kept whole rather than merged, because merging
prose neither author wrote would be composition.*


*Adopted 2026-08-23 (the CI-and-depth session, item 9). Law: `CLAUDE.md`, **Non-negotiables in code**. Supersedes nothing. It is the operation-count rule pointed at a BUILD STEP rather than at a data fetch — that rule asks an operation what it returned, and this asks a step what it produced.*

**Where a step's product can be looked at, look at it AT THE STEP. Not at the first thing that needs it.**

`main` went red and stayed red. Four tests failed with one message: *no browser is installed; I looked in this folder and found nothing.* The step before them — the one whose whole job is installing that browser — **reported success, in twenty-seven seconds**. Its own log, two screens above the failure, said it had downloaded the browser into exactly the folder the tests then searched.

The install was fine. **The thing doing the looking was broken**: it was looking for the browser file at the path an older version of the tool used, and the current version puts it somewhere else. It had been broken on every machine, including the author's own, for as long as it had existed.

Two things went wrong and they are separable:

- **A step reported success without its product being checked**, so the failure surfaced eighty seconds later, inside four unrelated tests, in a job that had already run a two-thousand-test suite.
- **The failure message pointed at the wrong half of the problem.** "No browser is installed" about a folder containing a freshly installed browser sends every reader to the installer, which was working perfectly.

So a step whose product can be observed gets a check right after it, and that check says what it looked for, where, and what it actually found. Where the thing the step produced can be compared against what the tool ITSELF says it produced, compare them — that comparison is what was missing here, and it is the only one that could have failed.

**And the check has no skip flag.** An escape hatch on a gate is how a gate stops meaning anything, and the one "fix" available locally — letting the check pass with no browser — is the exact thing the harness forbids in as many words.

---

</details>

## RULING 124 — a commit that cannot change what a reader sees does not cost a deploy

*`R-0124` · AMENDED · author_explicit · 2026-08-24 · also cited as `RULING 124`, `R124`, `R-124`*

- **amends** → `R-0078`
  - what changed: the ORCHESTRATOR runs once daily and each SOURCE inside it runs at the rate its own data moves, replacing RULING 78's flat once-daily cadence for every scheduled refresh
  - what survives, in force: RULING 78's rule that a gate running three times for one merge is one gate and two copies of it, and that nothing stops gating
- **sets** `shipping.closeout_path` = `no-separate-push`


*Adopted 2026-08-24 (Sean's instruction of that day, escalated twice: deploys are burning credits, cut them to the floor). Law: `CLAUDE.md`, **Stack**. Amends RULING 78, which set every scheduled refresh to once daily; the ORCHESTRATOR now runs once daily and each SOURCE runs at the rate its own data moves.*

**Six production deploys landed before 5 AM on 2026-08-24. Three of them rebuilt and redeployed a byte-identical application in order to serve paperwork.**

Reading the commits rather than counting them is what makes the finding obvious. `cdb5ce2` moved the meetings snapshot and `ccda6ea` moved the FEC snapshot — both are data a reader sees, and both deserved their build. `ba0947c` moved an intake report. `2a7e825` and `ae5b178` moved `docs/context.md` and `docs/state.md`. Nothing a reader can reach changed in any of those three, and each cost a full Next build and a deploy.

And that is only the visible half. Deploy previews are Netlify's default, so **every push to every session branch has been building too** — invisible in the production deploy list, and never looked at by anybody. The overnight session of 2026-08-24 alone pushed 15 branch commits.

**Five changes, and the last one closes the class:**

1. **Previews and branch deploys do not build.** The preview context was already closed in g17; the branch context was not, which left the same duplicate build running under a different name. Both are closed in `netlify.toml` now. `.github/workflows/build-check.yml` already runs the literal build command on every pull request, with a log readable without a Netlify login — which is the check the preview was standing in for.
2. **A path-keyed deploy filter.** `scripts/netlify-ignore.mjs` cancels a production build when every changed path is one that cannot change what a reader sees. The allowlist is `lib/ops/deploy-paths.ts`, with a stated reason per entry.
3. **One daily orchestrated refresh.** Five workflows on five crons committing five times becomes `refresh-daily.yml`: one run, per-source isolation, one gate, and **one commit however many sources moved**. A quiet day commits nothing at all — not a ceremonial "refreshed, no changes" commit, which is what was quietly being spent.
4. **Cadence matched to each source's real rate of change**, each with its reason stated on the entry: meetings and the NJ clerk filing daily through the election, FEC and LegiScan weekly, the federal `.gov` register monthly. Refreshing a barely-moving federal register every day burns a build to learn nothing.
5. **The close-out tool refuses a separate push to `main`.** Records ship inside the pull request. `scripts/close-out.mjs` had been made SAFE — it gates the build — and was still costing a full production deploy to serve a paperwork diff.

**THE ALLOWLIST DIRECTION IS THE RULE, and it keeps the cheap failure the only one available.** A path is paperwork only if it matches a named prefix. Everything else — every directory added tomorrow, every path this list has never heard of — is shipping, and builds. An unknown directory wrongly built costs one wasted build. An unknown directory wrongly classified as paperwork serves stale data to readers with nothing going red. Those are not comparable.

**`scripts/` is deliberately SHIPPING**, and it is the entry most likely to look like a mistake. Nothing under it reaches a reader — but `pnpm build` type-checks everything `tsconfig.json` includes, `scripts/` included, and RULING 76 exists because a session script broke the build. Cancelling that build would move the failure onto whichever unrelated commit built next.

**Every failure path builds.** No cached ref, a shallow clone, a git failure, the predicate failing to load — every one of them lets the build run and says why. RULING 24: a check that cannot reach its subject must never print like a passing one.

**The claim is measured rather than asserted.** `tests/deploy-paths.test.ts` reads the built `.nft.json` trace manifests — Next's own statement of which repo files each server bundle actually needs — and fails if any file under a non-shipping prefix appears in one. Re-deriving the classification from the list it was written from would prove only that the code is deterministic, which is RULING 114's lesson exactly. Measured on adoption: **31 trace manifests, 233 traced repo files, 0 under any non-shipping prefix.**

**And the cadence is calendar-driven on purpose.** The obvious implementation asks when an artifact last changed, with `git log -1 -- <path>`. That is wrong on CI and it fails silently: in a shallow clone, per-file `git log` returns the tip date for every file with no error, so a weekly source would read as refreshed-today every day forever.

---

## RULING 125 — verification happens on the local production build; production is the delivery truck, not the test bench

*`R-0125` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-24 · also cited as `RULING 125`, `R125`, `R-125`*

- **sets** `verification.target` = `local-production-build`


*Adopted 2026-08-24 (Sean's ruling of that day). Law: `CLAUDE.md`, **Non-negotiables in code**. It is RULING 77 — verify locally, ship once — carried to its conclusion: that ruling said WHEN to verify, and this says WHERE.*

**Every walk, every screenshot and every card check runs against a local production build. `walk:all` loses its production mode entirely.**

RULING 77 already established that almost nothing needs production, because a local production build is the same bytes. What it left standing was the habit: `walk:all` still defaulted to `https://sparkwtp.netlify.app`, and every session ended by walking the live site.

**The cost was never the traffic.** Every `/api/meetings` GET writes a row to the search log, and **the search log is a store this product sells.** A four-zip walk writes dozens; **11,755 synthetic rows** had accumulated in the production store by 2026-08-24. They are excluded from every aggregate by the `T10` machinery and that machinery works — but *organic by construction* is a stronger claim than *organic after filtering*, it is the claim the transparency page implies, and it costs nothing to have.

**The one remaining production fact is which SHA is live**, and it is read from **Netlify's deploy record via the API — one call, zero requests to the site.** Asking `/api/build` answers the same question while writing reader-indistinguishable traffic into a sold store, which is the thing this ruling exists to stop.

**And it is compared against the last DEPLOY-ELIGIBLE commit, never the tip of `main`.** Under RULING 124 a docs-only commit correctly never builds, so `main`'s tip is routinely a commit Netlify was right to ignore. A check comparing against the tip would report "production is behind" every time a close-out lands, forever — and an alarm that is wrong on every quiet day is an alarm nobody reads (RULING 115). `pnpm deploy:live` walks back to the newest commit the filter would have built, and compares that one.

**Four verdicts, and `cannot-tell` exits non-zero.** No Netlify credential is not a pass.

---

(Adopted 2026-08-24, Sean's ruling. It is **RULING 77 carried to its

**Every walk, every screenshot and every card check runs against a local

RULING 77 already established that almost nothing needs production, because a

**The cost was never the traffic.** Every `/api/meetings` GET writes a row to the

page implies, and it costs nothing.

**The one remaining production fact is which SHA is live**, read from **Netlify's
deploy record via the API — one call, zero requests to the site**. Asking
`/api/build` answers the same question while writing reader-indistinguishable
traffic into a sold store.

is routinely a commit Netlify was right to ignore; comparing against it would
report "production is behind" on every close-out, forever, and an alarm that is

## RULING 152 — a reader-facing DONE names the production deploy that is serving it

*`R-0152` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 152`, `R152`, `R-152`*


(Adopted 2026-08-25, earned by the reconciliation of Item 6. It is the
merge-cadence rule's missing receipt.)

**A session may not report a reader-facing item DONE without naming the
production deploy that carries it and the state that deploy reached.** Not the
merge, not the commit — the DEPLOY.

- **The deploy id, its state, and the SHA it built.** Read from Netlify's deploy
  API, which is one call and zero requests to the site (RULING 125).
- **A deploy that never reached `ready` has not shipped anything**, however
  green the merge was.
- **Where the deploy record cannot be read, the item reports `COULD_NOT_TELL`**
  and never DONE. RULING 24, applied to the last step.

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance.* The
reconciliation of 2026-08-25 tested six DONEs against what production was
actually serving during Sean's walk, and found **every claimed fix genuinely
live** — so this rule is not written because a deploy ate one. It is written
because ANSWERING the question took an afternoon and a Netlify token that was
not there a day earlier, and because the same read turned up four production
deploys in two days that reached `error` and were never published — `3449ef8`,
`41113c1`, `55d3047` and `e0f6426`. Three were real code merges. Each was
covered by a later merge so nothing was permanently lost, and **between the
merge and that later deploy production served older code while nothing in this
repo said so.** A receipt costs one API call and removes the question
permanently.

## RULING 155 — a session may not claim local gates green unless it ran the gate set CI requires, and named each one

*`R-0155` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 155`, `R155`, `R-155`*


(Adopted 2026-08-25, Sean's authority, from the recovery brief that followed
`RO04`. It is the operation-count rule — *an operation that can return nothing
must be asked what it returned* — pointed at the GATE SET rather than at a
single gate, and it is RULING 113's sibling: that ruling asks whether a step did
the thing, and this asks whether the step was ever run at all.)

**A session may not claim local gates green unless it ran the exact gate set CI
requires and named each gate with its individual result in its report.**

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance — and
here the rationale is a measurement rather than an argument.*

On 2026-08-25 the one-session-0825 run reported passing the full local gates:
**2,295 of 2,295 tests, `walk:all` exit 0, the deploy confirmed serving the
work.** It merged twice on that confidence. **`pnpm lint` was failing the entire
time**, on two `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` errors, and `main` was red
across both merges.

**The report was true about every gate it ran.** That is the whole finding.
Nothing in the repo asked it to run the one that was failing, because the local
door did not know that gate existed:

| | the local door ran | CI required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pnpm build` (default) | yes | yes |
| build, standalone mode | no | yes |
| `pnpm test` | no | yes |
| **`pnpm lint`** | **no** | **yes** |
| `tsc --noEmit` | no | yes |
| `assert:browser` | no | yes |
| `test:bundle` | no | yes |

`pnpm handoff --ship` calls itself the single door everything merges through and
`pnpm closeout` is RULING 75's gated door. **Both ran `pnpm run build` and
nothing else** — one of CI's seven commands. A session using either door
correctly, reporting honestly, still shipped red. **This is a hole in a door,
not a careless session**, and every session that used the door inherited it.

- **The local gate command is `pnpm gates`**, and it runs the set CI requires.
  Each gate is reported BY NAME with its own result, because a summary line
  cannot be written from a single aggregate boolean and "gates green" is exactly
  the sentence that was true and useless.
- **The gate set is anchored EXTERNALLY** (RULING 147).
  `tests/gate-parity.test.ts` reads `.github/workflows/build-check.yml` and
  fails when a command CI runs is absent locally. A check that re-derived the
  expected set from the local set would prove the file equals itself, and would
  have agreed with the hole every day it lived.
- **Every gate runs even after one fails**, mirroring the workflow's
  `if: always()`. A session gets all seven answers from one run rather than
  discovering them one merge at a time.
- **There is no skip flag**, for the reason the build gate already gives: an
  escape hatch on a gate is how the gate stops meaning anything.

*What the instrument taught about itself, recorded because it is the same class
of defect one floor up.* The first version of `scripts/gates.mjs` ran its gates
**on import**, so `tests/gate-parity.test.ts` importing the gate list executed
the whole suite — and the `process.exit()` at the end of that run killed the
test process after the first test. **A four-test file reported `pass 1, fail 0`
and a green tick.** It was caught by reading the run's own output rather than
its exit status: `test … PASS (1s)` for a 2,295-test suite is not a pass. That
is RULING 62's shape — a suite quietly reporting on fewer guards than it holds —
arriving through an imported side effect.

*And the parity test is shown catching the real hole* (RULING 110). Removing the
lint entry from the gate list fails two of its four assertions by name. A sweep
that cannot find the defect it was written for is a sweep reporting green about
nothing.

## RULING 156 — a required check is registered by NAME, and a rename disarms protection in silence

*`R-0156` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 156`, `R156`, `R-156`*


(Adopted 2026-08-25, closing `NS20` and `NS21`. It is RULING 155's shape one
floor up: that ruling closed a gate set with a hole in it, and this closes the
hole that would put a hole back in it without anyone editing a gate.)

**Sean hardened `main` himself on 2026-08-25, and it reads back from the GitHub
API exactly as intended.** `repos/SeanJ22/We-The-People/branches/main/protection`
returns, on that date:

| What the row asked for | What the API returns |
| --- | --- |
| PR required, approvals off | `required_pull_request_reviews` present, `required_approving_review_count: 0` |
| Three required contexts | `build (default)`, `build (standalone)`, **`gates (test · lint · tsc)`** |
| Branches up to date | `required_status_checks.strict: true` |
| **Do not allow bypassing** | **`enforce_admins.enabled: true`** |
| No force pushes, no deletions | `allow_force_pushes: false`, `allow_deletions: false` |

`NS20` asked for the gates job to become a required check and `NS21` asked for
bypassing to be turned back off. Both hold. **Both close on the API response**,
which is a server fact rather than a claim about the working tree (RULING 75's
third part, and RULING 125's reason for asking Netlify rather than the site).

**The hole underneath them is the NAME.** GitHub matches a required context
against the check-run name a workflow reports, as a literal string. Two of the
three are matrix legs — `build (${{ matrix.mode }})` — and the third carries a
middot-separated display name that a tidying edit would change without a second
thought. **Rename the job and the required context never arrives, and GitHub
does not treat that as a failure: there is nothing to wait for, so the merge
button turns green.** Protection disarms itself with nothing anywhere going red.

That is the same failure mode as the gate set RULING 155 was adopted over — a
check reporting nothing because it is not running, rather than a check that
fails — and it is worse here, because the disarming edit looks like tidying.

- **The anchor is the WORKFLOW FILE** (RULING 147). `REQUIRED_CONTEXTS` in
  `lib/ops/required-checks.ts` is a transcription of what the branch says;
  `contextsProducedByWorkflow` parses `.github/workflows/build-check.yml` and
  expands its matrix to derive what the workflow actually reports. Re-deriving
  one from the other would prove the file equals itself and would agree with a
  rename on every run, forever.
- **It fails in BOTH directions.** A required context the workflow no longer
  produces is protection disarmed; a check the workflow produces that the branch
  does not require is a gate nobody has to pass.
- **A rename is not forbidden — a SILENT rename is.** It has to move the
  workflow and the constant in one diff and then be re-registered on the branch.
  That is the mechanism `tests/guard-census.json` already uses to let a guard
  leave: leaving is allowed, leaving unnoticed is not.
- **A name this reader cannot resolve is REFUSED, never dropped.** A parser that
  quietly skipped an unexpandable job would under-report the produced set, and
  an under-reported set reads as agreement — RULING 100's partial, wearing a
  test's clothes.

*And the instrument is shown catching the real thing* (RULING 110). Three plants
run against the shipped workflow text: the gates job renamed to
`gates (test, lint, tsc)`, the `default` matrix leg renamed to `plain`, and a
job name carrying an expression the reader does not know. The first two drop a
required context; the third throws. `tests/required-checks.test.ts`, five
assertions.

---

## RULING 162 — a bypass is only as safe as the paths it can carry

*`R-0162` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 162`, `R162`, `R-162`*


**A scheduled workflow that pushes to `main` declares which paths it may write,
and the shared pusher refuses anything else. Fail closed, per workflow, with no
skip flag.**

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance.*
Hardening `main` on 2026-08-25 blocked all eight scheduled pushers, which push
directly. Sean ruled for a scoped bypass for the Actions bot — and **a bypass
that could carry code is the 8/25 hole reopened.** That hole was sessions
merging red code through PRs with nothing required; the actor was Claude Code
and the payload was code. The allowlist is what makes the payload structurally
incapable of being code, which is the only reason the bypass is acceptable at
all.

- **PER-WORKFLOW, not one global list.** A single list is the union of eight
  workflows' needs, so the FEC refresher would be permitted to write the ballot.
  Each profile grants exactly what its own workflow writes, so the blast radius
  of any one of them is one artifact.
- **It fails closed in FOUR directions**: an unknown or absent workflow id, a
  diff that could not be read, an **empty** diff, and any path outside the
  profile. The empty case is the one that looks harmless — a push of nothing is
  a path check with nothing to check, which is RULING 159's earned zero.
- **A second, independent list bars the dangerous prefixes outright**, so a
  profile widened by mistake still cannot admit `.github/`, `scripts/`, `lib/`,
  `tests/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/rulings.md` or the resolved tracker store.
  Re-deriving one list from the other would prove the file equals itself
  (RULING 147).
- **It lives in `scripts/push-main.mjs`**, the one script all eight already go
  through. Eight copies of a guard is eight places for it to drift, and a ninth
  pusher would inherit the copy nobody remembered to add.

**THE LIST IS DERIVED FROM WHAT THE PUSHERS ACTUALLY WRITE**, read off their own
`git add` lines, never from what they were expected to write. That reading is
what produced the finding: **`job-watch` ran `git add docs/` — the whole
directory — while needing exactly one file in it.** `docs/` holds `rulings.md`,
the resolved tracker store and every generated report, so anything left dirty in
the runner's tree by an earlier step would have been swept into a bot commit and
pushed to `main` unreviewed. Nothing had gone wrong yet; the blast radius was
simply far larger than the job's purpose.

**One grant sits outside `data/` and it is named rather than absorbed.**
`job-watch` may write `docs/tracker-working.csv`, because RULING 56 makes
committing the Needs Sean row its entire function, and that row is the only
channel that reaches a person when a scheduled job fails twice running. The
brief said the allowlist never includes the tracker stores; read strictly that
ends the alarm. The grant is made to one workflow for one file, reported, and
rowed for Sean to overrule (`NH204`).

`lib/ops/push-allowlist.ts`, guarded in `tests/push-allowlist.test.ts`, whose
load-bearing case is a workflow that did not exist when the guard was written:
a guardless pusher is constructed, caught, and gone when the test ends
(RULING 157).

## RULING 164 — a workflow reports every failure, not just the first

*`R-0164` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-26 · also cited as `RULING 164`, `R164`, `R-164`*


**Independent steps run to completion and report together. A genuinely
dependent step says "stopped here, N not attempted" rather than letting a
skipped step read as a passing one. And a `continue-on-error` step whose
outcome nobody reads is a swallowed failure.**

*The rationale.* Three failures were once stacked in run order in this repo,
each invisible until the one before it was fixed. **A workflow that reports only
its first failure makes the number of remaining defects unbounded** — nobody can
know how many lie between the current failure and the end, so every fix costs
another round trip through CI. It is the same family as every instrument defect
this repo has named: a mechanism reporting less than it knows.

*Measured on adoption: 9 workflows audited, 3 short-circuiting on independent
steps and 3 fixed, 6 legitimately dependent with the reason stated.*

- **`intake-tripwire`** ran three independent checks unguarded and in sequence —
  the schema gate, the write alarm and the tripwire — so the first failure ended
  the job. A schema that has drifted is precisely when the write alarm is most
  worth reading, so letting the gate suppress it is the wrong way round.
- **`refresh-daily`**'s go-red-for-failed-sources step lacked `always()`, so a
  validation failure hid which sources had failed. **Its sibling in
  `refresh-meetings-snapshot` already carried the guard** — an independent case,
  and the one that proves the correct form (RULING 157).
- **`refresh-nj-filing`** carried `continue-on-error: true` on the clerk-count
  reconciliation with **nothing reading `steps.pair.outcome` afterwards**, so a
  disagreement between the clerk's published count and what we render was
  swallowed whole and the run finished green. It stays non-blocking, as
  designed, and becomes visible.

**The general rule is the third one, and it is the class rather than the
instance** (RULING 136): `continue-on-error` converts a failure into a silent
pass, so any step carrying it must have its outcome read by something
downstream. `tests/workflow-failure-reporting.test.ts` sweeps every workflow for
it, asserts a floor so a reader that matched nothing cannot report green
(RULING 159), and is shown catching a planted one.

## RULING 165 — the scheduled pushers authenticate as a deploy key, and the private half is never held

*`R-0165` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-26 · also cited as `RULING 165`, `R165`, `R-165`*


**What this replaces, and why.** RULING 162 built a per-workflow path allowlist
to make a scoped bypass safe, on the assumption that the bypass would be granted
to the GitHub Actions app. **It cannot be.** A branch ruleset's `Add bypass`
list does not offer GitHub Actions as a selectable actor — confirmed by Sean
against the live UI on 2026-08-26, Apps tab filtered on `actions`, zero
suggestions. The community reports were right and the documentation was not.

So the bypass is granted to the **Deploy keys** category, and the eight
scheduled pushers stop using the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` over HTTPS.

**The cutover is in `scripts/push-main.mjs` and `lib/ops/deploy-key-ssh.ts`, and
nowhere else.** All eight pushers already routed through that one script. Eight
edits in eight workflows would be eight places to drift, and a ninth pusher
would inherit whichever copy nobody updated. *The one thing that could not live
there is the secret REFERENCE — `${{ secrets.* }}` is only expressible in
workflow YAML — so each pusher carries one plumbing line, and a test asserts all
eight carry it against a stated denominator, which turns eight lines into a
guarded invariant rather than eight places to drift.*

**Two facts about the bypass make the allowlist matter more than it did
yesterday, not less.**

- **It is CATEGORY-WIDE.** `bypass_actors` reports `DeployKey` with
  `actor_id: null`; there is no way to name a single key. Every write-enabled
  deploy key on the repository holds it. One is the intended state, and
  `pnpm protection:verify` now counts them and goes red at two.
- **Its mode is `exempt`, and that is Sean's settled decision.** An `always`
  bypass still EVALUATES the ruleset and waves the actor through afterward;
  `exempt` skips enforcement outright, which is what GitHub recommends for
  trusted high-volume automation and what a scheduled deploy-key push is. The
  consequence is stated rather than left implied: **an exempt key skips every
  rule in the ruleset, not only the ones that were blocking it. There is nothing
  left on the server between a scheduled job and `main`.**
  `lib/ops/push-allowlist.ts` is the whole of it, and it is unchanged and
  unweakened by this cutover.

**THE CREDENTIAL RULE SHAPED EVERY DESIGN DECISION, and it is absolute.** On
2026-08-25 a `curl` reporting flag printed nine credential values into a
transcript that mirrors to Drive, and all nine required rotation (RULING 127). A
private key is that failure with a worse blast radius. So:

- **No private key is generated, printed, echoed, or written by any session.**
  Sean generates the keypair locally, puts the public half in Deploy keys and
  the private half in the `PUSH_DEPLOY_KEY` secret. Code references the secret
  by name and never reads its value. **A design that would require a session to
  hold the private key is a wrong design and is changed.**
- **No diagnostic may carry key material.** Every refusal describes the key's
  SHAPE — absent, empty, missing its header, public half pasted by mistake — and
  the test proves it by handing in a marker and asserting it does not come back
  out.
- **The key file never lands in the repository or a synced folder.**
  `refuseUnsafeKeyRoot` turns that from a habit into a check, refusing rather
  than silently relocating.
- **It is removed on every exit path, the failure path included** — a `finally`
  around the push loop, proved through a declared seam because the real path
  needs a private key and a network call.
- **Even the tests hold no key.** A structural placeholder exercises every
  decision the module makes, which are all about shape and placement. Generating
  a throwaway keypair to make a test feel more real would put private-key
  material into a test run, a temp folder and a CI log.

**HOST VERIFICATION IS PINNED, NEVER DISABLED.** The obvious way to make an
unattended SSH push work is `StrictHostKeyChecking=no`, and that turns every
push into an unauthenticated one. `GITHUB_HOST_KEYS` is a DECLARED constant read
from GitHub's own `meta` endpoint — a value fetched at push time from the host
you are about to authenticate is not verification, it is a round trip. *Verified
against the live endpoint on adoption: `ssh -T git@github.com` with only these
keys pinned and no identity offered returned `Permission denied (publickey)`,
which means host verification SUCCEEDED and only authentication failed. A wrong
pin fails earlier and differently.*

**A MISSING CREDENTIAL IS A RED RUN AND MAY NEVER DEGRADE TO "NOTHING TO PUSH".**
That shape — a mechanism reporting success for work it did not do — has been
sighted enough times in this repo to have its own rulings (100, 113, 159). The
empty-string case is the one that matters: **in GitHub Actions an unset secret
interpolates to `""`**, so a check that only tested for `undefined` would sail
straight past a missing repository secret.

**The proof is both directions, on a real repository, through the command line
the workflows actually run.** A guard that refuses everything passes a refusal
test on its own. A commit carrying `scripts/anything.mjs` alongside the snapshot
is refused with the path named and origin's `main` unmoved; the same commit
without it lands. Asserting against `classifyPushPaths` would have proved that
the code the fix introduced does what the code does (RULING 153) — the guard is
wired in the direct-invocation block, so that is where it is exercised.

**And it is verified against a case it was not derived from** (RULING 157). The
cutover was derived from `refresh-daily`. The independent case is `job-watch`,
independent in the way that matters rather than in name: the only profile whose
grant lies outside `data/`, the only one whose allowlist is a single exact file
rather than a directory prefix, and the only pusher whose commit is an alarm
rather than an artifact.

*Measured on adoption: 1 of 1 write-enabled deploy key; `pnpm protection:verify`
INTACT, 9 of 9, against the live API; 8 of 8 pushers plumbed; 46 guards passing
across the three affected test files.*

## RULING 191 — one integration owner, one combined head, one merge at the end

*`R-0191` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-28 · also cited as `RULING 191`, `R191`, `R-191`*

- **extends** → `R-0190`
- **sets** `shipping.integration_model` = `one-owner-combined-head`

**A COMPLETED BRANCH IS NOT A COMPLETED SESSION.** RULING 190 fans the work
out; this is what the work comes back to.

**ONE INTEGRATION OWNER.** Exactly one branch owns canonical truth, the shared
governance artifacts, integration, combined verification and the final ship.
Parallel workstreams own their code, their tests and their own source data —
they do NOT each edit the shared stores. Canonical work state, the tracker
stores and workbook, the session state and log, the method store, and any
generated governance or canonical output are reconciled ONCE, by the integration
owner, in sequence.

**A branch changes canonical INPUTS. The integration owner regenerates the
OUTPUT once.** Letting each branch regenerate and commit a competing full-file
version of one generated artifact manufactures a conflict out of nothing and
violates RULING 92 on the way past.

**Shared load-bearing application files are decided BEFORE the fan-out, not
discovered after it.** Where two streams both need one such file, the session
picks deliberately: they are really one workstream; or one exposes an interface
the other depends on; or they modify separate regions and the ownership is
recorded. Discovering the dependency only after both branches contain broad
rewrites is the failure this clause exists to prevent.

**A workstream finishing means READY_FOR_INTEGRATION.** It does not merge to
`main`. Sub-workstream branches are implementation vehicles; the default
shipping topology is one final integrated PR from the integration branch.

**Branch-local green is necessary and not sufficient. Only the integrated head
is the product that ships.** After every integration, the focused overlap tests
for the stream just integrated run again; after all of them, the full local gate
set, the production build, the reader-visible controls, the source-denominator
checks and the generated-output checks run on the combined head — including the
interactions BETWEEN workstreams, which is the only place a combined head can
fail that no branch could.

**Where two branches conflict, neither "ours" nor "theirs" is an answer.** Both
branches were preserving an invariant. The integration owner re-reads both and
produces the combined behaviour.

This changes nothing about WHEN a merge happens. RULING 1 stands: verify
locally, accumulate, ship once at the real end, and the merge waits until the
session is ready to end rather than the session ending because the merge
happened.

## RULING 196 — an established migration is immutable, and correction is a new migration

*`R-0196` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-28 · also cited as `RULING 196`, `R196`, `R-196`*

- **sets** `schema.migration_mutability` = `immutable-append-only`

**A MIGRATION THAT EXISTS IN THE MERGE BASE MAY NOT BE MODIFIED, DELETED OR
RENAMED. CORRECTION IS A NEW MIGRATION.**

The schema shipping gate derives applied state from migration timestamps and
tags. That reading is only ever as good as an assumption nothing was checking:
**that a migration file is still what it was when it ran.** A rewritten
already-applied EXPAND migration stays "applied" by timestamp while the SQL
committed in Git is no longer the SQL the database executed — and every later
phase check then reasons from a file describing a state production was never in.
The gate would keep passing, and it would be passing about fiction.

**1. IMMUTABILITY IS CHECKED AT PR TIME AGAINST THE MERGE BASE**, and never
against commit dates. CI clones shallowly here, and per-file `git log` returns
the tip date for every file with no error at all — so a date-based check passes
while proving nothing, which is RULING 193's defect in a different subsystem.

**2. THE GENERATED JOURNAL AND THE FILES ON DISK MUST CORRESPOND EXACTLY.** A
journal entry with no file, or a file with no journal entry, is a failure.

**3. THE FAILURE NAMES THE FILE AND THE REMEDY.** "Correction requires a new
migration" is the whole instruction, and a gate that refuses without saying it
has taught the next session nothing.

**4. NOTHING HERE WEAKENS WHAT ALREADY WORKS.** Read-only production access, the
scoped PR and main gate, expand-before-contract ordering, the absence of a skip
flag, and the daily tripwire as defense in depth all stand exactly as they are.

## RULING 203 — the pure canonical authorities are gates, and a writer is never made one

*`R-0203` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-29 · also cited as `RULING 203`, `R203`, `R-203`*

- **extends** → `R-0155`

**`governance:check`, `orchestration:check` and `method:check` run in the
canonical gate set, named individually, in `pnpm gates` and in the required CI
job alike.** They were enforced only INDIRECTLY, by tests that assert things
about their subject matter — which is not the same as running them, and is the
RO04 shape exactly: a session runs every gate it knows about, reports all of them
green truthfully, and merges a ledger whose generated views are stale.

**Every candidate is CLASSIFIED BY READING IT before it is wired.** A pure
checker — one that reads canonical state, writes nothing, and exits non-zero on a
violation — may become a gate. **A mutating status, close-out or tracker writer
may NOT be run as a gate merely to make a question "covered".** A generator is
the sharpest case and is refused by name: running `governance:compile` as a gate
would have CI repair the staleness the gate exists to catch and go green having
destroyed its own evidence (RULING 92, RULING 102).

**One authoritative checker per question.** A second implementation is a second
verdict, free to disagree with the one branch protection already trusts.

## RULING 204 — production-integrity freshness fails closed, and the question is asked of what production SERVES

*`R-0204` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-29 · also cited as `RULING 204`, `R204`, `R-204`*

**A production-changing release may not proceed on an indefinitely stale
healthy reading.** `STALE_HEALTHY` did not freeze anything, so a green answer
about some earlier commit blessed every later one, forever.

**The subject of the freshness question is the commit production ACTUALLY
SERVES, never the candidate commit.** That distinction is the whole of the rule
and it was arrived at by rejecting the obvious alternative: a freeze keyed on the
candidate SHA can never be satisfied, because a post-deploy reading of a commit
cannot exist before that commit deploys, and the gate runs before the deploy.
**An unsatisfiable gate is the strongest argument anyone will ever have for the
skip flag this repository refuses to have.**

So the release gate ESTABLISHES what production serves — from the application's
own build endpoint, needing no credential — and then:

- served commit equals the recorded reading, within a stated maximum age →
  the reading is CURRENT FOR PRODUCTION and the release proceeds;
- served commit differs → production moved under our last reading. FROZEN;
- the reading is older than the bound, whatever the commits say → FROZEN;
- production cannot be ASKED → CANNOT TELL, which is FROZEN and is never a pass
  (RULING 24).

**The bound is an explicit parameter with no environment escape hatch and no
skip flag.** What survives unchanged from the owner's decision of 2026-08-28: a
red reading marks integrity DEGRADED, alerts, and blocks the next
production-changing release, and **nothing rolls production back** — the database
may already have advanced, and rolling code back underneath an advanced schema
manufactures a second incompatibility on top of the first.

**A deploy that never arrives is a fact about our build pipeline, never about
production's schema.** The observer records it as its own state and never as
`DEGRADED`, because a false failure class in a durable record freezes releases
for a reason that never happened.

## RULING 210 — the reader-answerability suite is the top-line health contract of the reader dimension

*`R-0210` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-30 · also cited as `RULING 210`, `R210`, `R-210`*

- **sets** `reader.health_contract` = `answerability-suite-with-typed-diagnostics`

The reader-answerability suite is the top-line health contract of the READER
dimension. It evaluates the owner-authored question corpus against the rendered
DOM of the pilot ZIPs. A red question automatically generates a TYPED DIAGNOSTIC
WorkItem carrying a failure class — acquisition, extraction, identity, linkage,
retrieval, evidence selection, synthesis, validation, rendering, accessibility,
interaction, or freshness — whose completion contract is that question turning
green. Red never defaults to "go acquire"; the failure class is diagnosed
first.

## RULING 211 — the known-answer control set is permanent, continuous, and unannounced

*`R-0211` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-30 · also cited as `RULING 211`, `R211`, `R-211`*

- **sets** `truth.control_standard` = `permanent-unannounced-control-set`

The known-answer control set is permanent, continuous, and unannounced. Control
facts are injected unlabeled into normal flow. It measures BOTH false absence
(denying a verified-present fact) and false presence (asserting a fact where
absence is verified). Negative controls carry their authority, period, and
verified-through scope. The set starts at roughly 40–60 owner-verified facts
across the four pilot ZIPs, weighted toward dangerous failure modes, and grows
continuously. A pre-activation test pass does not satisfy this ruling.

## RULING 212 — refresh cadence is derived from time-to-reader-impact and observed publisher change rate

*`R-0212` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-30 · also cited as `RULING 212`, `R212`, `R-212`*

- **supersedes_clause** → `R-0124`
  - what changed: the cadence half: RULING 124's one orchestrated daily run at hand-set per-source rates stops being the requirement. Cadence is now DERIVED from time-to-reader-impact and observed publisher change rate, no active obligation may have an unknown next-due, and the fixed daily floor survives only as a default for obligations with no better-derived cadence. The refresh.cadence claim moves to this ruling.
  - what survives, in force: everything else in RULING 124, entire: a commit that cannot change what a reader sees does not cost a deploy; previews and branch deploys do not build; the path-keyed deploy filter with its allowlist direction; scripts/ is deliberately SHIPPING; every failure path builds; the close-out tool refuses a separate push to main (shipping.closeout_path = no-separate-push); and the trace-manifest measurement of the classification.
- **sets** `refresh.cadence` = `derived-from-reader-impact-and-change-rate`

Refresh cadence is derived from time-to-reader-impact and observed publisher
change rate. The invariant is that no active obligation may have an unknown
next-due. The fixed daily floor is retired as a requirement and survives only
as a default for obligations with no better-derived cadence.

Transition rule (adopted with this ruling, shared with the freshness-clock
ruling adopted the same day): these are Level-2 activation invariants and
immediately govern the design, but their runtime satisfaction is intentionally
Session B work. Until Session B proves them, the FRESHNESS contract reports
NOT_READY; Session A does not widen scope merely to make the new invariant
green. Existing GitHub refresh jobs may remain temporarily as legacy runtime
while explicitly classified as non-authoritative and scheduled for Session B
replacement.

## RULING 217 — pilot health is three contracts rolled into one owner-facing reading

*`R-0217` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-30 · also cited as `RULING 217`, `R217`, `R-217`*

- **extends** → `R-0210`
- **extends** → `R-0211`
- **extends** → `R-0212`
- **sets** `health.pilot_rollup` = `three-contracts-one-rollup`

Pilot health is three contracts — READER (the suite), TRUTH (the control set),
FRESHNESS (staleness risk against reader-risk tolerance) — rolled into ONE
owner-facing PILOT HEALTH reading that is green only when all three are green.
No contract may certify another; no single contract may stand in for pilot
health.

## RULING 218 — GitHub scheduled workflows are not the freshness clock

*`R-0218` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-30 · also cited as `RULING 218`, `R218`, `R-218`*

- **extends** → `R-0212`
- **related_to** → `R-0124`
- **sets** `freshness.clock_authority` = `runtime-scheduler-derived-due`

GitHub scheduled workflows are not the freshness clock. Measured dispatch
delays (186–313 minutes typical, ~699 worst) are recorded evidence. GitHub
remains code CI, engineering safety, and at most a coarse backup wakeup. When
the runtime scheduler activates (Session B), ordinary civic-data movement
leaves the commit path. A late or failed scheduled dispatch is an
engineering/freshness defect — an operational incident and WorkItem — never a
Needs-Owner escalation by itself.

Transition rule (adopted with this ruling, shared with the derived-cadence
ruling adopted the same day): these are Level-2 activation invariants and
immediately govern the design, but their runtime satisfaction is intentionally
Session B work. Until Session B proves them, the FRESHNESS contract reports
NOT_READY; Session A does not widen scope merely to make the new invariant
green. Existing GitHub refresh jobs may remain temporarily as legacy runtime
while explicitly classified as non-authoritative and scheduled for Session B
replacement.

## RULING 233 — staging is the integration branch and deploys to the staging origin; promotion to main is earned against that exact head

*`R-0233` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-09-01 · also cited as `RULING 233`, `R233`, `R-233`, `R-C10`*

- **amends** → `R-0001`
  - what changed: the ROUTE a session's verified head takes to production: it merges to `staging` and is promoted to `main` through an exact-head gate, instead of merging to `main` directly. Not operative until the first session after Session C closes.
  - what survives, in force: RULING 1's merge cadence entire — verify locally, accumulate, ship ONCE at the real end, one code merge per session, close-out records following through their existing gated path, and the planned merge having happened never being a reason to stop.
- **related_to** → `R-0125`
- **related_to** → `R-0191`

**`main` is production and deploys to `meanwhileusa.com`. `staging` is
the integration branch and deploys to `test.meanwhileusa.com`.
`READY_FOR_INTEGRATION` heads merge to `staging` first under the existing
exact-head rule. Promotion `staging` → `main` occurs only when the canonical
reader suite, visual checks, and the walk pass against `test.meanwhileusa.com`
as a `STAGING_RENDER` target on that exact head, and the freeze gate is clear.
The production-integrity observer continues to verify `main` against
`meanwhileusa.com`; a second observer verifies `staging` against
`test.meanwhileusa.com`. Civic data is runtime and is not staged; only code
and schema changes flow through staging.**

## THE BOOTSTRAP CLAUSE, AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL

**This ruling is NOT OPERATIVE until the first session after Session C closes.**
The author was explicit about it, and the reason is that a shipping law cannot
first take effect inside the merge that installs it: the head that would be
promoted is the head that contains the promotion machinery, and nothing has yet
verified that machinery against a real staging deploy.

So, during Session C only:

- the `staging` branch may be created, and its ref may be fast-forwarded to
  the exact Session C integration head **solely to prove** the branch
  deployment, the staging database isolation, the observers, and promotion
  eligibility. **That is not a merge of code to `main`.**
- the promotion workflow **must be proved in exact-head eligibility/refusal
  mode**: a green exact staging head is ELIGIBLE; a stale, red, or
  wrong-database head is REFUSED. Proving the refusal branch matters more than
  proving the eligible one, because a gate that has only ever said yes has not
  been shown to be a gate.
- **it does not move `main`.** Session C's actual product shipment still uses
  the one planned RULING 1 merge from the integrated head to `main`.
- after that merge, `staging` may be fast-forwarded to the resulting `main`
  head so the next session begins synchronized.

## What it amends, and what survives untouched

RULING 1's merge cadence stands entire: verify locally, accumulate, ship once
at the real end, and the planned merge having happened is never a reason to
stop. What changes is the ROUTE that merge takes from the session's head to
production — through `staging` and a promotion gate rather than straight to
`main`.

**`PRODUCTION_RENDER` remains required for activation.** A `STAGING_RENDER`
run counts as `INDEPENDENTLY_REPRODUCED` for the purpose of earning
promotion; it does not become the production verification, and it may not be
recorded as one. That distinction is the same one RULING 125 draws between the
test bench and the delivery truck, with one more bench in between.

## Civic data does not stage

Only code and schema changes flow through staging. Civic data is acquired at
runtime against real publishers, and a staged copy of it would be a second
corpus with its own staleness, its own gaps and its own provenance — a
duplicate of the one store this product's whole claim rests on. The staging
database exists to isolate WRITES made by staging code, not to hold a rehearsal
copy of the record.

## The claim slot is deliberately left alone until this rule bites

`shipping.promotion_path` is declared in `lib/governance/claims.ts` and this
record does NOT claim it. That is not an omission. A semantic claim states what
is TRUE NOW, and until the bootstrap clause above expires the true answer is
still RULING 1's — the integrated head merges to `main`. A record that claimed
`staging-first-then-promotion` on the day it was adopted would make the
validator assert a shipping path that the very session adopting it is
forbidden to use.

So the slot is answered, and answered CORRECTLY: it is assigned to RULING 1
with the value `integrated-head-merges-to-main`. Declaring a rule slot and
leaving it empty would have been the worse failure — the acceptance gate counts
answered slots precisely so that a question nobody has answered cannot sit in
the ledger looking settled.

**The first session after Session C closes retires that assignment and lets
this record claim the slot**, and that reassignment — not this adoption — is
what makes this ruling operative rather than merely recorded.

## `package.json`'s `scripts` block is the list.

*`R-C-commands-package-json-s-scripts-block-is-the-list` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-20*

**`package.json`'s `scripts` block is the list.** (Rewritten 2026-08-20, Prompt
C item 4.3.) It held ten entries when this section was written by hand and
holds well over a hundred now, so any copy here is a copy that is wrong. Run
`pnpm run` to see them.

Four are named here because they are not conveniences — a rule elsewhere in
this file depends on each one existing and being run:

- **`pnpm stamp`** — today's date, `YYYY-MM-DD`, America/Phoenix. Every date
  entering every document comes from here. See the date rule below.
- **`pnpm verify-stamps`** — audits this file's own `Adopted` stamps against the
  git history that would have to be true for them, and writes
  `docs/stamp-audit.md` for the author to rule on.
- **`pnpm walk:all`** — the standing regression net, run against production at
  the end of every session. See the walk rule below.
- **`pnpm db:apply`** — applies the committed Drizzle migrations to a database
  this repo can reach. It is how a schema change reaches production, and
  `--target=production` is required to touch it.

## One CODE merge per session; close-out records may follow as separate named commits.

*`R-C-repo-layout-one-code-merge-per-session-close-out-records-may-fol` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-19*

**One CODE merge per session; close-out records may follow as separate named commits.** (Adopted 2026-08-19, the author's amendment to the merge cadence, after F01 shipped three merges under a rule that asked for one and reported the deviation rather than smoothing it.) The one-merge rule was always about CODE — batching reader-facing change into a single reviewable ship — and it collided with the sentence directly above: **a document cannot name the commit that contains it.** `docs/state.md` must carry the deploy SHA and the real `walk:all` numbers; neither exists until the code has shipped and been walked; writing either before it is known would be the fabrication rule, and chasing the regress would merge forever. So the line is drawn where it actually falls. The session ships its code ONCE. `state.md`, the tracker, and any document carrying the deploy SHA or the walk numbers may follow in separate commits, and the report states the **code SHA and the close-out record SHAs separately and labels them as such** — a reader must be able to tell at a glance which commit changed what a reader sees and which changed only our account of it. F01's `a119578` / `1203d48` / `5daeb8f` / `5253e5f` split is correct under this rule and is not a violation.

## The one exception, and it is the only one

*`R-C-repo-layout-the-one-exception-and-it-is-the-only-one` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-20*

**The one exception, and it is the only one** (amended 2026-08-20, the author's ruling): the session ships **one PLANNED code merge**. A SECOND code merge is permitted only to fix a regression the live walk caught — and when one is taken, the report **names the regression and states both SHAs**. That is the whole of the exception: not a second feature, not a second batch of items, not work that ran late. A walk that finds a live regression and a session that ships without fixing it is the worse outcome, and a rule that forced the choice would be a rule against fixing it. Any other second merge remains a deviation and is still reported as one. F01C2's `1407c53` / `7d986cb` split is correct under this amendment.

## This section names DECISIONS, never versions.

*`R-C-stack-this-section-names-decisions-never-versions` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-20*

**This section names DECISIONS, never versions.** (Rewritten 2026-08-20,
Prompt C item 4.3.) A framework version written here goes stale the next time
anyone runs an upgrade, and a stale constitution is worse than a short one — a
session reads it as current and builds against a fact that is no longer true.
So the shelf-life content lives where it is authoritative and this points at it:
**`package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`** for what is installed, **`netlify.toml`**
for how the deploy builds, **`next.config.ts`** for what the build does, and
**`drizzle.config.ts`** for the database wiring.

What does not drift, and is therefore law:

- Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript + React.
- Tailwind + shadcn/ui. The design tokens are committed — see the design-system
  rule below.
- Postgres on Neon, accessed through Drizzle. **Schema changes go through
  Drizzle migrations; no hand-edited SQL against the database**, and a
  migration is applied with `pnpm db:apply`.
- **Deployed on NETLIFY.** Not Vercel — the file said Vercel for months and it
  was never true of this repo. The build Netlify runs is the literal command in
  `netlify.toml`, and `.github/workflows/build-check.yml` runs that same string
  on every push so a refused build is readable without the author's Netlify
  login.
- **The scheduler is GitHub Actions, not platform cron.** **THREE workflows are
  SCHEDULED and EIGHT can push `main`, and the two numbers are different on
  purpose** (corrected 2026-08-24, RULING 124). The five data refreshers keep
  their `workflow_dispatch` and their push, so a source stays runnable by hand;
  what they lost is their cron. Every source's schedule now lives in
  **`refresh-daily.yml`** — one run a day, per-source cadence from
  `lib/ops/refresh-cadence.ts`, one gate, and **one commit however many sources
  moved**. The other two schedules, `intake-tripwire` and `job-watch`, commit
  only under `docs/`, which the deploy filter classifies as non-shipping, so
  **only one scheduled workflow in this repo can cost a production build.**
  The pusher count is asserted in `tests/push-main.test.ts` and the schedule
  census in `tests/refresh-cadence.test.ts`.

*The superseded text, kept because a deleted rule comes back as drift:* SEVEN
  workflows push `main` (corrected 2026-08-22, NJ Hunt 4 item 1, `NS02` — this line said
  five from the day it was written and was two short by the time anyone read
  it): `refresh-meetings-snapshot`, `refresh-fec-snapshot`,
  `refresh-legiscan-snapshot`, `refresh-dotgov-snapshot`, `intake-tripwire`,
  `job-watch` (added NH Hunt 3, RULING 56 — it commits the Needs Sean row it
  raises) and `refresh-nj-filing` (added NJ Hunt 3 — it rebuilds the Morris
  County ballot from the clerk's current filing). Each rebases and retries
  through `scripts/push-main.mjs`, because two of them running close together
  used to lose one run's work (R48). **The number is asserted in
  `tests/push-main.test.ts`**, so the next one to be added moves the test rather
  than quietly making this sentence wrong again. **Cadence is RULING 124's**,
  which amends RULING 78: the ORCHESTRATOR runs once daily, and each SOURCE
  inside it runs on the rate its data actually changes — meetings and the NJ
  clerk filing daily through the election, FEC and LegiScan weekly, the `.gov`
  register monthly, each with its reason stated on the entry. RULING 78's "every
  scheduled refresh runs ONCE DAILY, except the clerk filing" is superseded, and
  is kept here in that sentence rather than deleted.
- Auth via Auth.js, email magic link only — no OAuth, no social login.
- MapLibre GL with a vector tile provider. Not Google Maps.
- Mobile is responsive web first. A React Native client comes later if push
  notifications justify it, and will consume the same API.
